lines: {target}? Gentle ground can make travelers careless.
If anyone heads for Meadow, this is my advice. Rest there, but do not forget night comes.
Flowers and bees do not bar the dark.
Meadow is no small story.
I will remember Meadow as soft grass that still needs a lantern.
I would leave my route with someone before setting out for Meadow.
I would pack for Meadow with enough food, light, and patience.
Quiet would not persuade me that everything was safe at Meadow.
I would count a safe return as the finest prize from Meadow.
<shake>Pride</shake> makes a poor repair kit when things go wrong at Meadow.
Saving the tool comes second when open ground with nowhere to hide threatens the group.
Keep the right tool where you can reach it if a threat crossing the grass is part of the journey.
Once an open-country storm settles in, finding a hairline crack gets much harder.
A low wall sounds useful, but only if we can still use the road kept in sight.
On the open ground across Meadow, I would keep both hands free until the footing proved sound.
I expect the gear from Meadow to bring a lesson back to my workshop.
For another trip to Meadow, if the route demands climbing, every tool gets a tie before it gets packed.
Would you carry the same tools to Meadow after what happened there?
At Meadow, let the others count treasure. I'll count the tools that returned with us.
I'd like to see what Meadow did to the edge you carried.
{target}? Stone peaks make every fall honest.
If anyone heads for Stony Peaks, this is my advice. Bring blocks and stop before your legs shake.
Bare rock gives little cover and no softness.
Stony Peaks is no small story.
I will remember Stony Peaks as high stone with hard answers.
My first preparation for Stony Peaks would be telling someone the route.
I would bring steady light and enough food to turn back from Stony Peaks.
I would listen harder whenever the road went quiet near Stony Peaks.
I would rather return from Stony Peaks with a plain story than a fresh wound.
<shake>Pride</shake> makes a poor repair kit when things go wrong at Stony Peaks.
Before I followed that route, I would set aside a solid pick and blocks for steps.
Loose footing on a steep drop is the sort of trouble that punishes a rushed repair.
A fall with no easy rescue would be a poor time to discover the axe head was loose.
Even a simple repair gets clumsy when a mountain storm closes around you.
The stony climb above Stony Peaks sounds like a place for a light pack and tools tied down tight.
The scratches from Stony Peaks interest me almost as much as the story. Let me inspect them.
At Stony Peaks, I trust a plain tool that fits the hand better than a fine one that slips.
What suffered more at Stony Peaks, the iron or the handles?
Show me which tool stayed reliable through Stony Peaks. I may learn from its fit.
There is no shame in turning back when the repair kit starts looking too small around Stony Peaks.
{target}? Gravel moves when you most need it still.
If anyone heads for Windswept Gravelly Hills, this is my advice. Test every slope before trusting it.
Loose stone tells lies under boots.
Windswept Gravelly Hills is no small story.
I will remember Windswept Gravelly Hills as windy hills that slide under pressure.
The village should know my route before I travel to Windswept Gravelly Hills.
Food, torches, and a clear head belong in any pack for Windswept Gravelly Hills.
A quiet stretch is when I would grip the tools tighter near Windswept Gravelly Hills.
I want any tale of Windswept Gravelly Hills to end at home with supper.
<shake>Pride</shake> makes a poor repair kit when things go wrong at Windswept Gravelly Hills.
I would not ignore loose gravel sliding from steep wind-cut hills. Better to cross one unstable face at a time.
Tell me we are going to Windswept Gravelly Hills and I will start with a shovel and blocks for firm steps.
A mountain storm is no place to balance a loose rivet on one knee.
I would mark the lower ridge toward home before anyone stopped at a ledge out of the wind to repair gear.
I'd shorten every loose strap before stepping onto the windswept climb above Windswept Gravelly Hills.
I wonder what the repairs from Windswept Gravelly Hills will teach me at the bench.
A spare handle is light compared with a broken-tool walk back from Windswept Gravelly Hills.
Has that journey changed the kit you would take back to Windswept Gravelly Hills?
What did you put on the repair bench first after Windswept Gravelly Hills?
At Windswept Gravelly Hills, every tool gets a tie before I trust it on a climb.
{target}? Hard wind turns every edge into advice.
If anyone heads for Windswept Hills, this is my advice. Keep low and do not race the mountain.
Clouds move fast up there and so can mistakes.
Windswept Hills is no small story.
I will remember Windswept Hills as high rough land that talks in gusts.
Before visiting Windswept Hills, I would make sure someone expected my return.
Good provisions matter more than a heavy pack on the way to Windswept Hills.
The calm moments would keep me watchful during a trip to Windswept Hills.
I would make room for the story, not another scar from Windswept Hills.
<shake>Pride</shake> makes a poor repair kit when things go wrong at Windswept Hills.
Hearing about high broken ridges catching every hard gust makes me want to stay below the crest when the wind rises.
A light pick and rope for the pack would be a sensible start for Windswept Hills.
The thought of a fall with no easy rescue is enough to make me pack a second working tool.
Any adjustment that can wait until after a mountain storm should wait.
The windswept climb above Windswept Hills would tell me which tool stays packed and which one stays ready.
I would not send gear back out after Windswept Hills without looking over every joint.
There is no shame in turning back when the repair kit starts looking too small around Windswept Hills.
I am already reconsidering which tools belong on a trip to Windswept Hills.
After hearing about Windswept Hills, I'd oil the iron and test every wedge twice before leaving.
For Windswept Hills, I'd bring wedges, cord, and enough iron for one ugly repair.
